advisor.summary: Section 79 excludes the cost of the first $50,000 of employer-provided group term life coverage from the employee's income. Coverage above that imputes income at the age-banded Table I rates of Reg. §1.79-3(d)(2) — rates that often undercut actual premiums for older insureds — and the imputed amount is FICA wages. The employer deducts premiums under §162(a) so long as it is not a policy beneficiary. The dollars are deliberately small: this is a hygiene item bundled into a broader fringe redesign, not a headline strategy. But it is cheap and very commonly done wrong — §1372 denies the exclusion to >2% S corporation shareholders, and a plan favoring key employees forfeits their $50,000 exclusion under §79(d).
mechanics: The §79 exclusion requires true group term coverage carried by the employer — generally ten or more full-time employees, or the small-group alternative of Reg. §1.79-1 that covers all eligible employees on a formula basis.

Coverage above $50,000 imputes income at the Table I uniform premium of Reg. §1.79-3(d)(2), reduced by employee after-tax contributions; the imputed cost is reported in W-2 Box 12 code C and constitutes FICA wages.
Because Table I rates sit below actual term pricing at older ages, even the taxable slice can be a rate arbitrage against personally owned coverage for insureds in their fifties and sixties.

Entity mapping is the compliance core: C-corp owner-employees qualify like any other employee, while §1372 treats >2% S corporation shareholders as partners — their premiums belong on the W-2 with no §79 exclusion — and partners and sole proprietors are not employees at all.

The employer deducts premiums under §162(a) only while it holds no beneficial interest in the policy — §264(a)(1) forecloses the deduction otherwise — and a plan favoring key employees costs them the exclusion under §79(d).

authority.note: The exclusion for the cost of the first $50,000 of group term coverage, the imputation above that line, and the §79(d) nondiscrimination rules.
The Table I uniform premiums — the age-banded rates that impute income on coverage over $50,000.
Defines group term life coverage, including the under-ten-employee alternative rules.
Treats >2% S corporation shareholders as partners: no §79 exclusion, and their premiums are W-2 wages.
Denies the employer's deduction where the employer is, directly or indirectly, a policy beneficiary.
The employer's premium deduction as ordinary compensation expense whenever §264 does not apply.

requirements: A group term policy carried by the employer covering an eligible class — ten or more employees, or a compliant small-group formula design.
Employees as the insureds, naming their own beneficiaries; the employer holds no beneficial interest.
Table I imputation and FICA on coverage above $50,000, coded correctly through payroll.
A §79(d) nondiscrimination review wherever key employees participate.
risks: The leading audit finding is S corporation misclassification: >2% shareholders claiming the §79 exclusion that §1372 denies them — a payroll correction with years of quiet W-2 errors behind it, grounded squarely in the statute rather than case law.
Owner-tilted small-group designs fail §79(d), stripping key employees of the $50,000 exclusion and imputing income at the greater of Table I or actual cost.
Coverage above $50,000 left unimputed accrues W-2 and FICA errors that surface in payroll exams.
The benefit is a few hundred dollars of premium per person — oversell it and the plan's credibility suffers. It belongs in a bundle, not on a cover page.
stateNotes: Conformity: federal-AGI states conform to the §79 exclusion and the Table I imputation with no adjustment.

PTET: for S corporation and partnership sponsors, the premium deduction reduces the entity income a PTET election is computed on; there is no separate owner-level PTET effect, because >2% shareholders and partners sit outside the exclusion anyway.
Missouri: conforms through RSMo §143.121; the $50,000 exclusion and any Table I imputed income carry onto the Missouri return exactly as computed federally.
reviewChecklist: Group status verified under Reg. §1.79-1, or the small-group alternative documented in the file.
Owner premiums mapped correctly by entity type — no §79 exclusion for >2% S-corp shareholders.
Payroll system imputes Table I on coverage above $50,000, using current age bands.
Employer confirmed as a non-beneficiary on every certificate.

client.teaser: Up to $50,000 of life insurance per employee — tax-free to them, deductible to the company.
client.headline: Life insurance your company can give tax-free
plainEnglish: The tax law lets your company give each employee up to $50,000 of term life insurance with no tax to the employee. The company deducts the premiums. It is one of the simplest benefits there is.

To be straight with you: this is a small-dollar item. The savings are the tax on a modest premium. We include it because it costs little, employees value it, and it is often set up wrong — especially for S corporation owners, who follow different rules.
Want more than $50,000 of coverage? The extra is taxed using an IRS rate table. For older employees, that table often beats the cost of buying term insurance on their own.
client.analogy: This is the tax version of tightening a loose screw — quick, cheap, and worth doing while the toolbox is already out.
benefits: Tax-free coverage for every employee, deductible to the business
The IRS rate table can beat retail term prices for older insureds
A low-cost benefit employees actually notice
steps: WE review how any current life coverage runs through payroll.
WE fix the owner treatment if it is wrong — a common finding.
YOU approve the coverage design; the payroll handling runs itself from there.
clientCommitments: Keep us posted on new hires and coverage changes so the payroll reporting stays right

annualMaintenance: Confirm Table I imputation is running on current age bands
Re-check §79(d) discrimination as the census changes
Verify owner premium mapping after any entity change
deliverables: Annual compliance checklist for the file
